title: Why did Amundsen beat Scott to the South Pole?
subject: histoire
description: In 1911, a Norwegian and a Briton set out at the same time for the southernmost point on the planet. Dogs, skis and furs on one side, ponies, motors and man-hauling on the other: everything came down to preparation.
author: elizabeth-singer-hunt

hero.hook: Two teams set out for the same spot on the globe a few weeks apart, and only one came back alive.

blocks.text: The early 1900s were the Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration (**1895-1922**): expedition after expedition, adventurers pushed deeper into the white continent. The prize: the South Pole, at **90° south latitude**. Despite the attempts of Robert Falcon Scott in 1902 and Ernest Shackleton in 1909, nobody had reached it.

In **1911**, two teams set out for it at the same time, one British, the other Norwegian. Both would reach their goal, but only one would come back alive. This race mixed planning, cunning, luck and willpower, qualities that were not all on the side of the survivors.

The Norwegian Roald Amundsen is said to have spent more than ten years preparing for the career of polar explorer. An expert skier and dog handler, he sailed through the [[Northwest Passage]] between **1903 and 1906** and lived alongside the [[Netsilik]] Inuit, learning from them how to dress, travel and survive in extreme cold.

blocks.caption: Roald Amundsen in a fur parka.

blocks.text: He first set his sights on the North Pole. But when the Americans Frederick Cook and Robert Peary claimed to have reached it before him, in **1909**, he secretly changed his target. In 1910, his ship, the [[Fram]], set sail with **97 dogs** and 19 men. He revealed the true destination, the South Pole, only in Madeira, three months later. To Scott, already on his way, he telegraphed: "Beg to inform you Fram proceeding Antarctic. Amundsen." The race was on.

sections.title: Scott and the lesson of the Discovery

blocks.text: A Royal Navy officer, Robert Falcon Scott already knew Antarctica: in **1901**, he led the [[Discovery expedition]], a major scientific mission to the continent. The British had little experience with skis or sled dogs, but on **2 November 1902**, Scott, Ernest Shackleton and Edward Wilson set off with 19 dogs toward the Pole.

blocks.caption: Shackleton, Scott and Wilson in front of the Discovery, 1902.

blocks.text: They nearly lost their lives. The dogs weakened, probably in part because they were fed rotten fish, and the men had to haul their heavy sledges themselves. Hunger set in, and Shackleton developed [[scurvy]]. On **December 30**, they turned back at 82°17' south, about **460 miles** from the Pole. Scott came away convinced of the merits of human willpower: conquering Antarctica by one's "own unaided efforts" made the prize more "nobly and splendidly won." He wanted to try again.

sections.title: Dogs versus ponies: the race begins

blocks.text: Amundsen set up his base in the [[Bay of Whales]], about **60 miles** closer to the Pole than Scott, despite facing an uncharted route. On **20 October 1911**, he set out with four companions, all expert skiers, four sledges and **52 dogs**. The men skied alongside the sledges, and dogs would be slaughtered along the way to feed the men and the surviving animals.

Amundsen wore loose-fitting reindeer-skin furs: the Inuit had taught him that they trap warmth while letting air circulate. Scott's men layered wool under windproof clothing, which trapped perspiration and became dangerously cold. Scott himself wondered whether Inuit clothing might "outclass our more civilised garb."

Scott's plan was broader. From McMurdo Sound, his expedition began its push south on **1 November** with 16 men, **10 ponies**, 22 dogs and two motor sledges. The motors broke down and the ponies struggled: the men ended up hauling almost everything themselves, as in the days of the Discovery. For the final push, Scott kept Wilson, Oates, Evans and Bowers.

On **14 December 1911**, Amundsen and his companions reached the South Pole. Scott's team got there **34 days** later, on 17 January 1912, and found the Norwegian flag waiting, a crushing blow after months of marching. Scott called it a "disaster." The Norwegians, for their part, returned safely after **99 days** and nearly 1,900 miles: well-placed depots, seasoned skiers and dogs, and unusually mild conditions on the plateau explain their success.

blocks.caption: Scott, Wilson, Oates, Evans and Bowers at the South Pole, January 1912.

blocks.text: Scott's return turned into a fight for survival: extreme cold, hunger, despair. Evans died first, then Oates deliberately walked out into the blizzard. Scott, Wilson and Bowers struggled on until a storm trapped them **11 miles** from One Ton Depot. On **29 March**, Scott wrote: "we are getting weaker of course, and the end cannot be far." Their bodies were found in November 1912.
The Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station, an American research base at the South Pole, today bears the names of both rivals, reunited at the very spot they were racing to reach.

events.title: The Discovery turns back
events.detail: Scott, Shackleton and Wilson give up at 82°17' south, 460 miles from the Pole.

events.title: The Fram sets sail
events.detail: Amundsen reveals his true destination, the South Pole, only in Madeira.

events.title: Amundsen at the Pole
events.detail: Five Norwegians, four sledges and their dogs reach 90° south.

events.title: Scott at the Pole
events.detail: The British find the Norwegian flag, 34 days too late.

events.title: Last page of the diary
events.detail: After nearly 1,500 miles, much of it hauling their own sledges, Scott writes his final words.

blocks.text: Amundsen won through preparation: skis, dogs, furs and depots learned from the Inuit, while Scott bet on ponies, motors and the strength of men.
